passages.happening:
Jesus crosses the lake back to his own town, Capernaum. Some men bring him a paralyzed man lying on a mat. Seeing their faith, Jesus says to the man, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.”

Some scribes think to themselves, ‘This man is blaspheming.’ Jesus knows their thoughts. Which is easier, he asks, to say ‘Your sins are forgiven’, or to say ‘Get up and walk’? So that they may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he tells the man, “Get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” The man gets up and goes home. The crowds are filled with awe and praise God, “who had given such authority to men.”
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story at more length (Mark 2:1-12), with the crowded house and the friends digging through the roof. Matthew leaves those details out and keeps the two things that matter most to him: the word of forgiveness and the healing that backs it up.

The scribes, teachers of the Law, are not being petty. They know that sin is first of all against God, and that only God can forgive it. To blaspheme meant to speak against God or to claim what belongs to him, and the Law treated it as a grave crime (Leviticus 24:16). If Jesus is not who he claims to be, the scribes are right to be alarmed. The same charge will be brought against Jesus at his trial, when the high priest tears his clothes and says, “He has blasphemed!” (26:65).

Then the test. Anyone can say ‘Your sins are forgiven’; no one can see whether it worked. But ‘Get up and walk’ can be checked at once. Jesus does the thing that can be seen to show the authority of the thing that cannot.

Only Matthew ends with the crowd praising God for giving such authority ‘to men’. Some readers think he is already looking ahead to the authority Jesus gives his followers to ‘bind’ and ‘loose’ (16:19; 18:18).
passages.hard:
Did the man's sin cause his paralysis? Many people in Jesus' day assumed that sickness came from sin. Jesus does not say so here. In John's Gospel, when the disciples ask about a man born blind, “who sinned, this man or his parents”, Jesus answers, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:2-3). Jesus begins with forgiveness because it is the deepest need every person has, not because this man was worse than others.

Whose faith did Jesus see? Matthew says ‘their faith’: most readers take it to mean the faith of the men who carried him, and perhaps his own. Friends can bring someone to Jesus who cannot get there alone. As the note on 8:1-4 says, these stories never teach that those who stay sick lacked faith.
passages.asks: The men who carried the mat are never named, but Jesus saw their faith. Who are you carrying? And which do you want more from Jesus: to be forgiven or to be fixed? He gave this man both, but he gave forgiveness first.

passages.t: A tax collector called, and a meal with sinners
passages.happening:
As Jesus goes on, he sees a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, and Matthew gets up and follows him.

Later Jesus is eating at Matthew's house, and many tax collectors and ‘sinners’ come and eat with him and his disciples. The Pharisees see it and ask the disciples, “Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus hears and answers, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” Then he sends them back to the prophet Hosea: “But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
passages.hearers:
Capernaum sat near the border between the lands of Herod Antipas and his brother Philip, on a road used by traders. The man at the tax booth was most likely a toll collector, taking customs on goods for Antipas. Tax collectors had a reputation for taking more than was owed; when some came to John the Baptist, he told them, “Collect no more than you are authorized” (Luke 3:13). Many Jews saw them as traitors who grew rich off their neighbours. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, later allowed a person to make a false vow to protect his goods from murderers, robbers, and tax collectors. That is how low the trade stood.

Mark and Luke call this man Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27). Matthew calls him Matthew, and in the list of the twelve apostles it adds ‘the tax collector’ (10:3). Most readers think Levi and Matthew were two names for one man, as Simon was also called Peter. From early in the second century the church linked this Gospel with him.

‘Sinners’ did not mean everyone, though everyone sins. It meant people known for living outside God's law. To share a table in that world was to accept the people at it. The Pharisees were a movement devoted to keeping God's law carefully in daily life, including at meals, and they were respected by ordinary people. Their question is a real one: what does it say about a teacher if he eats with people like these?

Jesus answers with a proverb that was known well beyond Israel. The Greek writer Diogenes Laertius tells of the philosopher Antisthenes, blamed for keeping bad company, replying that doctors attend the sick without catching their fever.
passages.ot:
Hosea spoke for God to a people whose loyalty to him came and went: “your loyalty is like a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes” (Hosea 6:4). Then: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6). The word for ‘mercy’ is the Hebrew hesed: loyal love, kindness that keeps faith.

The prophets were not against the sacrifices the Law commanded. They were against worship without kindness. Samuel had said, “obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22), and Micah asked, “what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). Matthew is the only Gospel to quote Hosea 6:6, and he quotes it twice (here and 12:7).
passages.hard:
Is this scene fair to the Pharisees? It is easy to make them the villains of every story, as if they cared only for rules and nothing for people. That picture is unfair, and Christians have used it to look down on Jews and Judaism.

Jewish teaching has always held that God forgives those who turn back to him. Through Ezekiel God asks, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” (Ezekiel 18:23). Jewish tradition treasured Hosea 6:6 too. A collection of rabbinic teaching written down long after the Gospels, Avot de-Rabbi Natan, tells how Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai, after the temple was destroyed in AD 70, comforted a student by citing this verse: acts of loving-kindness bring atonement as the sacrifices had. So Jesus is not setting a Christian idea against Judaism. He quotes a Hebrew prophet in an argument among Jews about how far God's welcome reaches.

The sharp edge is in the last line: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” Jesus does not mean that some people are good enough not to need him. People who think they are healthy do not call a doctor. The warning is for anyone, in any religion, who is sure of their own standing and uneasy about whom God lets in.
passages.asks: Matthew's first act as a follower of Jesus was to throw a dinner and invite his friends. Ask whom you would be uncomfortable seeing at Jesus' table, and why. And ask the harder question: where do you think of yourself as one of the healthy, who do not need the doctor?

passages.happening:
John the Baptist's disciples come to Jesus. They ask why they and the Pharisees fast often, but Jesus' disciples do not.

Jesus answers with a picture. Wedding guests cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them. “But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” Then two more pictures: no one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old coat, and no one pours new wine into old wineskins. “Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”
passages.hearers:
The law of Moses commanded only one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Other fasts grew up later; Zechariah mentions fasts in four different months (Zechariah 8:19). Many devout Jews fasted more. In one of Jesus' parables a Pharisee says, “I fast twice a week” (Luke 18:12). Fasting was a sign of serious faith, and of mourning and longing for God to act.

John's disciples had good reason to mourn: their teacher was in prison (4:12). Their question is sincere.

A wedding in a Jewish village was a feast that could last a week; Samson's lasted “seven days” (Judges 14:12). The bridegroom's friends were expected to celebrate, not to fast.

The other two pictures come from daily life. New cloth shrinks the first time it is washed, so a new patch tears away from an old coat. Wine was kept in skins of leather. New wine is still fermenting and stretches its container. An old skin is dry and stiff, and it bursts.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus do away with fasting? No. He says that his followers will fast once he is ‘taken from them’, the first hint in Matthew that he will die. The early church did fast. An early Christian manual called the Didache, from around AD 100, tells believers to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays.

What are the old wineskins? Readers differ. Some think of the customs of Jewish piety, which could not simply hold the new thing Jesus brought. Others note that in modern Bibles only Matthew has ‘both are preserved’: the new wine is kept, and so are the skins it is put in. On that reading Jesus is not throwing the old away but finding a fitting home for the new. Matthew's Gospel, which says Jesus came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (5:17), may want both thoughts held together.
passages.asks: There is a time to feast and a time to fast, and Jesus says the difference is whether he is near. Ask which season you are in. And ask whether you are trying to pour something new God is doing into an old container that cannot hold it.

passages.t: A dead girl, and a woman who touched his cloak
passages.happening:
While Jesus is speaking, a synagogue leader kneels before him. “My daughter has just died,” he said. “But come and place Your hand on her, and she will live.” Jesus gets up and goes with him.

On the way a woman who has suffered from bleeding for twelve years comes up behind him and touches the fringe of his cloak. She has told herself that if she only touches his cloak, she will be healed. Jesus turns and sees her. “Take courage, daughter,” He said, “your faith has healed you.” She is well from that hour.

At the leader's house Jesus sees the flute players and the noisy crowd. “Go away,” He told them. “The girl is not dead, but asleep.” They laugh at him. When the crowd has been put outside, he takes the girl by the hand, and she gets up. The news spreads through the whole region.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Luke tell this double story at length and name the father Jairus (Mark 5:21-43). Matthew tells it in nine verses. The notes on Mark 5 explain much that a first hearer would catch.

Under the Law, a woman with a long flow of blood was ritually unclean for as long as it lasted (Leviticus 15:25-27). ‘Unclean’ does not mean sinful or dirty. It meant she could not come near to worship at the temple, and people who touched what she lay or sat on had to wash. Scholars debate how cut off from daily life this made her. Matthew says nothing about uncleanness at all. What he stresses is her twelve years of suffering and her faith.

The ‘fringe’ was most likely one of the tassels that God told Israelite men to wear on the corners of their clothes, to “remember all the commandments of the LORD” (Numbers 15:39). Jesus dressed as a faithful Jew. Later, whole crowds beg to touch the same fringe (14:36).

Mourning began at once when someone died. Families hired flute players and women who wailed. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, records a rule that even a poor man must provide at least two flute players and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral. The Jewish historian Josephus says that when a false report of his own death reached Jerusalem during the war with Rome, many people hired flute players to lead their laments. The laughter at the house came from people who had no doubt the girl was dead.
passages.ot:
Calling death ‘sleep’ is an old way of speaking in Scripture, used with hope. Daniel says, “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2). Jesus does not mean the girl was only in a coma. He means that for him, death is something a person can be woken from.

Elijah and Elisha had each raised a dead child (1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 4:32-37), and each did it by crying out to God and stretching himself over the child. Jesus simply takes her hand.
passages.hard:
In Mark and Luke, the father says his daughter is dying, and messengers come later to say she has died (Mark 5:23, 35). In Matthew he says from the start, ‘My daughter has just died.’ Does Matthew contradict them?

The difference is real. Augustine, in his Harmony of the Gospels, said that Matthew, telling the story briefly, put into the father's mouth what had in fact become true by the time Jesus reached the house; the substance is the same. Many modern scholars add that ancient writers of lives often shortened stories and joined scenes together without meaning to deceive. Some readers point out that Matthew's change makes the father's faith greater still: he asks Jesus not to heal a sick child but to raise a dead one. Skeptical readers see a sign that the Gospel writers felt free to change their sources. The difference is plain on the page, and readers can weigh it for themselves.
passages.asks: Both people in this story come with nothing left: one with a child already dead, one with twelve years of failed cures. Jesus did not send either away. Ask what you have stopped bringing to him because it seems too late. And notice that he called the woman ‘daughter’ in front of everyone.

passages.happening:
As Jesus goes on, two blind men follow him, crying out, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!” When he goes into the house, they come to him. “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” He asked. “Yes, Lord,” they answered.

He touches their eyes and says, “According to your faith will it be done to you.” Their eyes are opened. Jesus warns them sternly to let no one know. But they go out and spread the news all over the region.
passages.hearers:
‘Son of David’ was a title for the promised king. God had told David that a descendant of his would rule, and that God would “establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). Matthew's Gospel opens by calling Jesus “the son of David” (1:1), and it uses the title more than any other Gospel. These blind men are the first people in Matthew to call out to Jesus by it. They cannot see him, but they see who he is.

Blindness was common in the ancient world, from infections, injury, and poor care, and many blind people lived by begging.

This is the second time Matthew tells of two people where we might expect one. He does it again with two blind men at Jericho (20:30), where Mark tells of one, Bartimaeus. The notes on 8:28-34 set out how readers explain this.
passages.ot: Isaiah had promised a day when God would come to save his people: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy” (Isaiah 35:5-6). In these two short stories, the blind see and the mute speak. When John the Baptist later asks whether Jesus is the one to come, Jesus points to exactly these signs (11:4-5).
passages.hard:
‘According to your faith will it be done to you.’ Does that mean that people who are not healed did not believe enough? No. Jesus was answering these two men, who had just said they believed. It is not a rule that measures every sick person's faith by whether they get well. As the note on 8:1-4 sets out, Scripture shows faithful people who stayed ill, and it never blames them.

Why tell them to keep quiet? Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a wonder-worker, or to be swept up by crowds who wanted a king of the wrong kind. The men disobey, out of joy. Their story shows how hard it is to keep good news to yourself.
passages.asks: Jesus asked the two men a plain question: do you believe I can do this? Ask what you would answer if he asked you the same thing about the need you carry. And if your honest answer is ‘I want to’, that is a place to start.

passages.t: A man who could not speak
passages.happening:
As the two men leave, people bring Jesus a man who cannot speak, troubled by a demon. When the demon has been driven out, the man begins to speak. The crowds are amazed. “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!”

But the Pharisees say, “It is by the prince of demons that He drives out demons.”
passages.hearers:
The Greek word for the man (kōphos) means ‘blunted’ or ‘dull’, and it can mean deaf, or unable to speak, or both. Here the point is that he could not speak, and then he could.

The two answers to the same deed stand side by side. The crowds say nothing like this has ever happened in Israel. Some of the Pharisees say it is the devil's work. No one in the story denies that something happened. The question is where the power came from.

The charge outlived Jesus. In the second century the Christian writer Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho, says that some opponents called Jesus a magician and a deceiver of the people. An accusation like that does not deny that Jesus did unusual things. It tries to explain them.
passages.hard:
Was the man's silence caused by a demon, or was he simply unable to speak? Matthew tells of a demon here. Elsewhere he tells of mute people healed with no mention of demons (15:30-31), and he lists the demon-possessed and the sick as different needs (4:24). The Gospel itself does not teach that every disability or illness has an evil spirit behind it, and it would be wrong and cruel to say so of anyone today.

The charge in verse 34 is the start of a longer argument. In chapter 12 the Pharisees say it again, and Jesus answers it at length (12:24-32).
passages.asks: Two groups saw the same thing and drew opposite conclusions. Ask what makes the difference between seeing God at work and explaining it away. And ask whether there is someone in your life whose voice has gone quiet, and who needs someone to listen.

passages.t: Sheep without a shepherd, and a plentiful harvest
passages.happening:
Jesus goes through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness. When he sees the crowds, he is moved with compassion for them, because they are harassed and helpless, “like sheep without a shepherd.”

Then he says to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.”
passages.hearers:
Verse 35 repeats almost word for word the summary in 4:23. Matthew uses the two summaries like bookends. Between them stand the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5 to 7), Jesus' words, and the ten miracles of chapters 8 and 9, Jesus' deeds.

The word for ‘moved with compassion’ comes from a Greek word for the inner parts of the body, the gut. It describes a feeling that moves a person from deep inside.

Sheep without a shepherd wander, get hurt, and are easy prey. Most people in Galilee were farmers, fishermen, or labourers. They knew sheep, and they knew harvest: the short, urgent weeks when the crop is ripe and every pair of hands is needed before it is lost.
passages.ot: When Moses asked God for someone to lead Israel after him, he prayed that “the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd” (Numbers 27:17). Ezekiel spoke against Israel's leaders, who fed themselves and not the flock: “They were scattered for lack of a shepherd” (Ezekiel 34:5). In the same chapter God promises to shepherd his people himself, and to set one shepherd, ‘My servant David’, over them (Ezekiel 34:15, 23). Matthew wants the reader to see that promise being kept.
passages.hard: If the harvest belongs to the Lord, why does he need workers, and why must they ask him to send them? Christians have always found this a mystery: God does his work, and he does it through people, and he wants to be asked. The prayer comes first. Then, in the very next verse, Jesus calls his twelve disciples and sends them out. Those who pray for workers often find that they are the answer.
passages.asks: Jesus looked at crowds and felt compassion, not irritation. Ask how you see the crowds you pass every day. Then pray the prayer he gave, for workers in the harvest, and be ready to be one.
